docs.title: Connection forward
docs.text:
• Note 4 extends mean and variance to vectors: the mean becomes a vector, the variance becomes the covariance matrix, and together they describe a multivariate Gaussian completely.
  • Notes 7 and 8 define entropy and KL divergence as expectations of \(\log p\). Every information quantity in this series is an expectation.
  • Note 11 writes maximum likelihood as maximising an expectation over the data, estimated by a sample average, as in the code above.
  • Note 19 designs the forward process with the rule \(\mathrm{Var}(aX + \sigma\varepsilon) = a^2 \mathrm{Var}(X) + \sigma^2\), choosing \(a^2 + \sigma^2 = 1\) at every step.
  • Note 23 trains a network by squared error to predict the clean image (or the noise) from the noisy image. By Proposition 3.6, what it learns is a conditional expectation.
  • Note 26 shows that this conditional expectation and the score of the noisy distribution are the same information in two forms.

docs.title: From Jensen's inequality to the ELBO
docs.text:
Sessions. A note takes one topic at a time. A session page follows one line of argument across several topics, in the order that worked best when friends and I went through the material together. This one runs through convexity, Jensen's inequality, KL divergence, maximum likelihood, latent variables and the ELBO.

Prerequisites: notes 1, 2 and 3.

docs.title: Where this page is going
docs.text:
The goal is to make a model distribution \(p_\theta\) close to the distribution of the data. To say what "close" means we need a way to measure how far apart two distributions are. That is the KL divergence. The one fact about the KL that everything rests on, that it is never negative, is proved with a single inequality, Jensen's. So the page builds those two tools first (sections 1 and 2), and then follows the argument:

  1. Learning the data distribution means maximum likelihood (section 3).
  2. A network cannot output a density directly (section 4).
  3. A hidden variable gets around that, but its likelihood is an integral we cannot compute (section 5).
  4. The ELBO is a lower bound on that likelihood which we can compute (sections 6 and 7), and it becomes the training loss (section 8).

The same bound, applied to a chain of hidden variables, is how DDPM is trained. That comes on a later page.

docs.title: 1. Jensen's inequality
docs.text:
In many derivations we end up comparing two quantities: a curved function applied to an average, and the average of that function. Jensen's inequality tells us which of the two is larger.

A chord joins two points on the graph of \(\log\). As a weighted average slides between them, the graph stays above the chord. With probabilities as the weights, the same picture says \(\log \E[U] \ge \E[\log U]\): the log of an average is at least the average of the logs.

docs.title: 1.1 Curved functions, and the form that defines them
docs.text:
Draw the graph of \(\log u\) for \(u > 0\). It rises, but more and more slowly: it bends downward. Pick any two points on the graph and join them with a straight segment, a chord. The chord always lies below the graph. A function with this property is called concave. The function \(e^u\) bends the other way: every chord lies above its graph. Such a function is called convex.

To turn the picture into a formula we need to name a point between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\). Take a weight \(\lambda\) between \(0\) and \(1\) and form

\[ \lambda\, a + (1 - \lambda)\, b . \]

This is a weighted average of \(a\) and \(b\). Its two coefficients, \(\lambda\) and \(1 - \lambda\), are not negative and add up to one. That is what keeps the result between \(a\) and \(b\): it equals \(a\) when \(\lambda = 1\), \(b\) when \(\lambda = 0\), and the midpoint when \(\lambda = \tfrac12\).

Definition (concave and convex)

\(f\) is concave if for any two points \(a, b\) and any weight \(\lambda\) between \(0\) and \(1\),

\[ f\big(\lambda a + (1 - \lambda) b\big) \;\ge\; \lambda f(a) + (1 - \lambda) f(b). \]

\(f\) is convex if the inequality goes the other way, \(\le\).

The left side is the height of the graph above the point \(\lambda a + (1 - \lambda) b\). The right side is the height of the chord above the same point. So the definition says "graph above chord". The same weights appear on both sides, once inside \(f\) and once outside: for a concave function, the function of the average is at least the average of the function.

Drag \(a\) and \(b\) under the plot, and move the weight \(\lambda\). The orange marker on the axis is the weighted average of \(a\) and \(b\). Above it, the ring is the height of the graph and the diamond is the height of the chord. For \(\log\) the ring is always above the diamond. Switch to \(e^u\) or \(u^2\) and it is always below.

The same holds for any number of points \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\), as long as the weights \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n\) are not negative and add up to one:

\[ f\big(\lambda_1 a_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n a_n\big) \;\ge\; \lambda_1 f(a_1) + \cdots + \lambda_n f(a_n) \qquad (f \text{ concave}). \]

A combination \(c_1 a_1 + \cdots + c_n a_n\) with any coefficients is a linear combination. A weighted average is the special case with coefficients that are not negative and sum to one, and its formal name is a convex combination.

docs.title: 1.2 Log is concave, exp is convex
docs.text:
A function whose second derivative is never positive is concave; never negative, convex. The second derivative measures bending: negative means the slope is decreasing, so the graph bends down.

function second derivative so it is \(\log u\), for \(u > 0\) \(-1/u^2 < 0\) concave \(e^u\) \(e^u > 0\) convex \(u^2\) \(2 > 0\) convex \(a u + b\) \(0\) both: a straight line is its own chord

With numbers. For \(\log\), take \(a = 1\), \(b = 4\) and equal weights. The function of the average is \(\log 2.5 = 0.916\). The average of the function is \(\tfrac12(\log 1 + \log 4) = 0.693\). The first is larger, as concavity says.

For \(e^u\), take \(a = 0\), \(b = 2\). The function of the average is \(e^1 = 2.72\). The average of the function is \(\tfrac12(e^0 + e^2) = 4.19\). Now the first is smaller, as convexity says.

docs.title: 1.3 An expectation is a weighted average: Jensen's inequality
docs.text:
An expectation is a weighted average

\[ \E[U] = p(u_1)\, u_1 + p(u_2)\, u_2 + \cdots + p(u_n)\, u_n \]

The probabilities are not negative and add up to one. So an expectation is a weighted average of the values of \(U\), with the probabilities as the weights.

Example. The number of heads in two tosses: \(\tfrac14 \cdot 0 + \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 = 1\), with weights \(\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14\).

Put the values \(u_i\) in the place of the points \(a_i\) and the probabilities in the place of the weights. The left side of the many-point form becomes \(f(\E[U])\) and the right side becomes \(\E[f(U)]\):

Jensen's inequality

For any random variable \(U\):

\[ f \text{ concave:}\quad f\big(\E[U]\big) \;\ge\; \E\big[f(U)\big], \qquad\qquad f \text{ convex:}\quad f\big(\E[U]\big) \;\le\; \E\big[f(U)\big]. \]

If \(f\) is strictly curved, equality holds only when \(U\) is constant.

For a straight line the two sides are equal: that is the rule \(\E[aU + b] = a\E[U] + b\) of note 3. The numbers of section 1.2 were two cases of Jensen, with \(U\) equal to \(1\) or \(4\), and to \(0\) or \(2\), with probability \(\tfrac12\) each.

In the illustration below, each ▲ handle under the plot is one equally likely value of \(U\). The navy dots are the values \(f(u_i)\). Their average, the orange diamond, sits at horizontal position \(\E[U]\) and height \(\E[f(U)]\). The ring on the graph directly above it is at height \(f(\E[U])\). The teal segment between them is the Jensen gap.

Drag the handles. With \(f = \log u\) the diamond is always below the ring; with \(u^2\) or \(e^u\), always above. Pull the points apart and the gap grows; bring them together and it shrinks to zero. Then press show the tangent line, which is the proof below.

Proof: the tangent line

Write \(\mu\) for the number \(\E[U]\). This is just a name, which keeps the random \(U\) apart from the one fixed point \(\mu\) where we draw a tangent. For a concave \(f\) the tangent line at \(\mu\) lies above the graph everywhere:

\[ f(u) \;\le\; f(\mu) + f'(\mu)\,(u - \mu) \qquad \text{for every } u . \]

This holds for every value \(U\) can take, so it holds on average. The right side is a straight line in \(u\), so its expectation is easy:

\[ \begin{aligned} \E\big[f(U)\big] &\le \E\big[f(\mu) + f'(\mu)(U - \mu)\big] && \text{average of an inequality that holds everywhere} \\[4pt] &= f(\mu) + f'(\mu)\,\big(\E[U] - \mu\big) && f(\mu),\ f'(\mu) \text{ are fixed numbers} \\[4pt] &= f\big(\E[U]\big) && \E[U] - \mu = 0 . \qquad \square \end{aligned} \]

The tangent lies above a concave graph by Taylor's theorem: \(f(u) = f(\mu) + f'(\mu)(u - \mu) + \tfrac12 f''(\xi)(u - \mu)^2\) for some \(\xi\) between \(\mu\) and \(u\), and the last term is \(\le 0\) when \(f'' \le 0\).

Two familiar inequalities follow directly from Jensen's inequality.

  • Variance is never negative. For the convex \(u^2\), Jensen gives \(\E[U^2] \ge (\E[U])^2\). The difference of the two sides is exactly \(\mathrm{Var}(U)\) (note 3). So the Jensen gap for \(u^2\) is the variance.
  • The arithmetic mean is never below the geometric mean. For positive \(a\) and \(b\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, Jensen for \(\log\) gives \(\log \tfrac{a + b}{2} \ge \tfrac12(\log a + \log b) = \log \sqrt{ab}\), so \(\tfrac{a + b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}\). For \(1\) and \(4\): \(2.5 \ge 2\).

Variance is never negative, line by line.

The arithmetic mean is never below the geometric mean.

Which way does the inequality go?

A convex function, like \(u^2\), is shaped like a bowl. A chord across a bowl hangs above the bottom, so the average of the values is the larger side: \(\E[f(U)] \ge f(\E[U])\). For \(u^2\) this is the statement that the variance \(\E[U^2] - (\E[U])^2\) is never negative, which is easy to recall.

A concave function, like \(\log\), is shaped like a dome. The chord sits under it, so the inequality flips: \(f(\E[U]) \ge \E[f(U)]\).

A quick check with numbers for \(\log\), using \(1\) and \(4\) with equal weights: the log of the average is \(\log 2.5 = 0.92\), and the average of the logs is \(\tfrac12(\log 1 + \log 4) = 0.69\). The log of the average is larger, as the dome says.

docs.title: 1.4 Where a log meets an expectation
docs.text:
In machine learning we often work with the logarithm of a probability. The probability of a dataset is a product over many data points, and taking the log turns that product into a sum, which is much easier to handle. We also often take expectations, because some quantities are unknown or random, such as the data point, a hidden variable or the noise, and we average over them. As a result, expressions that contain both a \(\log\) and an \(\E\) come up all the time, and the order matters: the log of an average is not the same as the average of the logs. Since \(\log\) is concave, Jensen's inequality tells us which one is larger:

\[ \log \E[U] \;\ge\; \E[\log U] . \]

We will use this inequality twice on this page: to prove that the KL divergence is never negative (section 2), and to bound a log-likelihood we cannot compute (section 6).

docs.title: 2. KL divergence
docs.text:
Often we need to compare two distributions: a model with the data, for example, or an approximation with the distribution it is meant to approximate. The KL divergence is a way to measure how different two distributions \(q\) and \(p\) are.

To build it, take a single point \(z\) and compare how probable it is under each distribution. The log of the ratio \(q(z)/p(z)\) is positive where \(q\) gives \(z\) more probability than \(p\) does, negative where it gives less, and zero where the two agree. The KL divergence is the average of this log-ratio, with \(z\) drawn from \(q\).

Definition (Kullback–Leibler divergence)

\[ \KL(q \,\|\, p) = \E_{z \sim q}\!\left[ \log \frac{q(z)}{p(z)} \right] = \sum_z q(z) \log \frac{q(z)}{p(z)} \quad\text{or}\quad \int q(z) \log \frac{q(z)}{p(z)}\, \d z . \]

The distribution in the first slot is the one we average over.

Example. Let \(p\) be a fair coin and \(q\) a coin that shows heads with probability \(0.9\):

\[ \KL(q \,\|\, p) = 0.9 \log \frac{0.9}{0.5} + 0.1 \log \frac{0.1}{0.5} = 0.529 - 0.161 = 0.368 . \]

The tails term is negative. Individual terms can be negative; the total cannot. Swapping the roles gives \(\KL(p \,\|\, q) = 0.5 \log \tfrac{0.5}{0.9} + 0.5 \log \tfrac{0.5}{0.1} = 0.511\), a different number. The KL is not symmetric.

KL is never negative

\[ \KL(q \,\|\, p) \;\ge\; 0, \qquad \text{with equality exactly when } q = p . \]

Proof, with Jensen. Minus the KL flips the ratio inside the log. Then apply Jensen to the concave \(\log\):

\[ \begin{aligned} -\KL(q \,\|\, p) &= \E_q\!\left[ \log \frac{p(z)}{q(z)} \right] && -\log a = \log \tfrac{1}{a} \\[4pt] &\le \log \E_q\!\left[ \frac{p(z)}{q(z)} \right] && \text{Jensen: } \log \text{ is concave} \\[4pt] &= \log \sum_z q(z)\, \frac{p(z)}{q(z)} = \log \sum_z p(z) = \log 1 = 0 . && \square \end{aligned} \]

Equality in Jensen needs \(p(z)/q(z)\) to be the same constant \(c\) wherever \(q\) has mass; both add up to one, so \(c = 1\) and \(p = q\).

The same proof, one line at a time.

Since the KL is not symmetric, it is not a distance in the geometric sense. A useful way to read \(\KL(q \,\|\, p)\) is as a measure of how badly \(p\) explains samples that come from \(q\).

Samples come from \(q\) and stay fixed. The model \(p\) moves until it explains them, and the KL falls to zero. This is the first row of the table below: fitting a model to data, with the data in the first slot.

Between two Gaussians the KL has a closed form:

\[ \KL\big( \N(m_1, v_1) \,\|\, \N(m_2, v_2) \big) = \frac12 \left[ \log \frac{v_2}{v_1} + \frac{v_1 + (m_1 - m_2)^2}{v_2} - 1 \right]. \]

When the two variances are equal, the log term vanishes and what is left is a squared distance between the means:

\[ \KL\big( \N(m_1, v) \,\|\, \N(m_2, v) \big) = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)^2}{2 v} . \]

This second formula is what later turns the DDPM objective into the mean-squared-error loss used in practice.

docs.title: Which side do we adjust?
docs.text:
In the definition, the samples come from the distribution in the first slot, and the distribution in the second slot is scored on how well it explains them. Which of the two we adjust depends on the problem, and this page has both cases.

first slot: where the samples come from second slot: scored on explaining them what we adjust fitting a model to data (section 3) the data the model \(p_\theta\) the second slot a proxy for a posterior (section 6) the proxy \(q\) the true posterior the first slot

The first row is the common and intuitive one: the samples are given, and the model moves until it explains them. In the second row the thing we adjust sits in the first slot, for a practical reason: we can only average over a distribution we can draw samples from. In both cases, the first slot holds the distribution we can draw samples from, and we adjust whichever of the two is ours.

docs.title: Seeing the KL
docs.text:
The illustration shows the second row: the navy curve is a target \(p\), the orange curve is a Gaussian \(q\) that we adjust. The lower panel plots \(q(z) \log \tfrac{q(z)}{p(z)}\); its total area is \(\KL(q \,\|\, p)\).

Move \(q\) with the sliders. The KL is never negative and reaches zero only when the orange curve lies on the navy one. Then switch to two bumps and press the two minimise buttons.

With a two-bump target no single Gaussian fits, and the two directions disagree about which comes closest. Minimising \(\KL(q \,\|\, p)\) puts \(q\) on one bump: averaging over draws from \(q\), any mass \(q\) puts in the empty valley is punished heavily, so it settles for one bump (mode-seeking). Minimising \(\KL(p \,\|\, q)\) gives a wide Gaussian covering both bumps (mass-covering). The ELBO of section 6 uses the first, mode-seeking direction.

Why the logarithm? Why not compare q(z) and p(z) directly?

The log turns ratios into differences, and "how many times more likely" is the natural comparison for probabilities: being wrong by a factor of 2 should count the same at \(10^{-1}\) as at \(10^{-6}\). Logs also make independent pieces add up: for independent coordinates, the KL of the joint is the sum of the KLs. And \(-\log p(z)\) is the "surprise" of seeing \(z\) when you expect \(p\), so the KL is the extra surprise you suffer, on average, by believing \(p\) when the samples come from \(q\).

docs.title: 3. The goal: what it means to learn the data distribution
docs.text:
The goal is to make \(\log p_\theta(x)\) large, but a network cannot give that density directly. A hidden variable turns it into an integral we cannot compute, and a proxy \(q\) turns the integral into a bound we can: the ELBO, whose gap to the true value is a KL divergence. Its negative is the training loss.

We have samples from an unknown distribution \(p_{\text{data}}(x)\). We want a distribution \(p_\theta(x)\) with adjustable parameters \(\theta\) that we can bring close to \(p_{\text{data}}\), and a way to draw new samples from it.

With the KL divergence we can say what "close" means: we want \(\KL(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_\theta)\) to be small. The data sits in the first slot because the data is what we can draw samples from. The formula contains \(p_{\text{data}}\), which we do not know. Writing it out shows how much of it we actually need:

\[ \KL(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_\theta) = \underbrace{\E_{\text{data}}\big[ \log p_{\text{data}}(x) \big]}_{\text{unknown, but contains no } \theta} \;-\; \underbrace{\E_{\text{data}}\big[ \log p_\theta(x) \big]}_{\text{an average over data}} . \]

The first term does not change whatever we do to the model. The second is an average over data, and data is what we have. So raising the second term lowers the KL, and we never need \(p_{\text{data}}\).

Result (maximum likelihood)

Making \(\KL(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_\theta)\) small is the same as making

\[ \E_{x \sim \text{data}}\big[ \log p_\theta(x) \big] \;\approx\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log p_\theta(x_i) \]

large, where \(x_1, \ldots, x_N\) are the training examples.

Note that the logarithm was not our choice; it came out of the KL. One limitation is that the first term stays unknown, so we can tell which of two models is closer to the data, but not how far the better one still is. What we need from the model, then, is a way to compute \(\log p_\theta(x)\) for a data point.

If we do not know p_data, how can we take an expectation over it?

We never need its formula, only samples from it, and the training set is exactly that: a collection of samples from \(p_{\text{data}}\). An expectation under \(p_{\text{data}}\) is the long-run average of a quantity over draws from it, so averaging the same quantity over the training examples gives an estimate of it, and the estimate improves as the dataset grows (the law of large numbers). That is the \(\approx\) in the box above. The first term of the KL is different: it needs the value \(p_{\text{data}}(x)\) at each sample, which we do not have, and this is why it stays unknown. Fortunately it does not contain \(\theta\), so we can leave it alone.

docs.title: 4. Can a network output the density directly?
docs.text:
Neural networks are flexible functions, so a natural first idea is to let a network \(f_\theta\) take \(x\) and return a density. A density must be non-negative, which \(e^{f_\theta(x)}\) arranges, and it must integrate to one, which needs a division:

\[ p_\theta(x) = \frac{e^{f_\theta(x)}}{Z_\theta}, \qquad Z_\theta = \int e^{f_\theta(x)}\, \d x . \]

\(Z_\theta\) is an integral over all of data space, a million dimensions for a small image, of a function defined by a network. It has no formula, cannot be computed on a grid, and changes every time \(\theta\) changes. Without it we cannot evaluate \(p_\theta(x)\), which is exactly the ability section 3 asked for.

Two ways around \(Z_\theta\) come back later in the series. Differentiate: \(\nabla_x \log p_\theta(x) = \nabla_x f_\theta(x)\) does not contain \(Z_\theta\), and that gradient is the score of Part V. Or split \(x\) into coordinates and model one at a time, each a one-dimensional distribution that is easy to normalise, which is how language models work. On this page we take a third route and do not write \(p_\theta(x)\) down directly.

Two simpler attempts: a formula, and a table

A formula, such as a Gaussian with fitted mean and covariance, is easy to fit and to sample, but it is one bump, and no choice of parameters bends a bump into a spiral (left panel).

A table: cut the plane into cells and count. It takes any shape (middle panel), but with \(10\) cells per coordinate a tiny \(28 \times 28\) image needs \(10^{784}\) cells, and the table gives probability zero to everything not in the training set. To learn from finite data, what we learn about one \(x\) must tell us something about nearby \(x\): a function with shared parameters, a network.

The right panel belongs to section 5: noise pushed through a transformation.

docs.title: 5. A way around: a hidden variable
5.1 Describe how a sample is made
docs.text:
Instead of writing the distribution down, we can describe how a sample is produced.

A small example. A friend has two coins in a pocket, one fair and one that shows heads \(90\%\) of the time. Each round the friend picks one without showing you, flips it, and tells you only the result. Which coin was used is a hidden variable: it shaped the result, and it is never in the data.

A latent-variable model is the same idea with a continuous hidden variable and a network:

  • a prior \(p(z)\) over the latent \(z\), almost always \(\N(0, I)\);
  • a decoder \(p_\theta(x \mid z)\), a distribution over data given a latent, with a network inside.

To generate, draw \(z\) from the prior and then \(x\) from the decoder. The joint is \(p_\theta(x, z) = p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)\), and we only ever observe \(x\). The model is flexible and easy to sample from, but \(p_\theta(x)\) itself does not appear anywhere in this description.

The example for this page. One latent number and one data number:

\[ z \sim \N(0, 1), \qquad x \mid z \sim \N(w z,\; s^2), \qquad w = 1,\ s = 0.8 . \]

Draw \(z\), multiply by \(w\), add Gaussian noise. Here every quantity has an exact formula, so each claim can be checked against the truth. A real VAE replaces \(wz\) by a network, and then nothing has a formula.

Is the hidden variable something real, like the coin in the pocket?

In the coin story it is a real cause. In a VAE or in DDPM it is a modelling device: "hidden" only means it has no observed values in the data. Nothing guarantees that a learned \(z\) means "slant" or "thickness"; whatever meaning it has comes out of training. In DDPM the hidden variables will be noisy versions of the image, which are not in the dataset because we invent them.

docs.title: 5.2 The likelihood is an integral
docs.text:
The probability the model gives to \(x\) is the marginal, with the latent summed out (note 2):

\[ p_\theta(x) = \int p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)\, \d z . \]

Go through every latent, ask how likely it is and how likely it is to produce this \(x\), and add up. In the example, \(x = wz + s\varepsilon\) is a sum of independent Gaussians with variance \(w^2 + s^2 = 1.64\), so for \(x = 1.5\)

\[ \log p(x) = -\tfrac12 \log(2\pi \cdot 1.64) - \frac{1.5^2}{2 \cdot 1.64} = -1.852 . \]

Everything below is compared with this number. For a network decoder with a latent of many dimensions, the integral has no closed form and cannot be done on a grid.

Why not estimate the integral by sampling z from the prior?

In one dimension it works: averaging \(p(x \mid z)\) over 20 000 prior samples gives \(\log p(x)\) between \(-1.84\) and \(-1.87\). But in many dimensions only a tiny region of latent space produces anything like a given \(x\), and a latent drawn from the prior almost never lands there. The fix is to sample \(z\) from a distribution that knows about \(x\), which is the posterior of the next section.

docs.title: 5.3 The posterior, and a proxy for it
docs.text:
Given \(x\), which latents could have produced it? That is the posterior (note 2):

\[ p_\theta(z \mid x) = \frac{p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)}{p_\theta(x)} . \]

The denominator is the integral we cannot compute. But the numerator can be computed for any \(z\), and the denominator does not depend on \(z\). So we know the posterior's shape; only its scale is missing. In the example it is \(\N(0.915,\ 0.390)\) for \(x = 1.5\).

Since the true posterior is out of reach in general, we bring in a proxy: a distribution \(q(z)\) of our own, simple enough to sample from and evaluate, usually a Gaussian with an adjustable mean and variance. In a VAE a second network, the encoder, produces it.

We only want to generate. Why do we need the direction from x to z?

For training. To improve the decoder on a data point \(x\), we need to know which latents should have produced it, so we can push the decoder's output for those latents toward \(x\). In DDPM this direction comes for free: it is the noising process.

docs.title: 6. The ELBO
docs.text:
Fix one data point \(x\) and any proxy \(q(z)\). Each line uses one fact:

\[ \begin{aligned} \log p_\theta(x) &= \E_{q}\big[ \log p_\theta(x) \big] && \log p_\theta(x) \text{ does not depend on } z \\[4pt] &= \E_{q}\!\left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)} \right] && \text{definition of the posterior} \\[4pt] &= \E_{q}\!\left[ \log \left( \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)} \cdot \frac{q(z)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)} \right) \right] && \text{multiply and divide by } q(z) \\[4pt] &= \underbrace{\E_{q}\!\left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)} \right]}_{\text{ELBO}} \;+\; \underbrace{\E_{q}\!\left[ \log \frac{q(z)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)} \right]}_{\KL(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x))} && \text{log of a product is a sum} \end{aligned} \]

Result (the ELBO identity)

\[ \log p_\theta(x) \;=\; \text{ELBO}(q, \theta) \;+\; \KL\big( q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x) \big) \;\ge\; \text{ELBO}(q, \theta), \]

since the KL is never negative. ELBO stands for evidence lower bound; "evidence" is an old name for \(p(x)\).

  • The ELBO is computable. It needs only the joint \(p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)\) and our own \(q\), and it is an expectation under \(q\), so it can be estimated by sampling from \(q\).
  • The gap is exactly the KL from \(q\) to the true posterior. If \(q\) is the posterior, the bound is an equality.
  • The left side does not depend on \(q\). So raising the ELBO through \(q\) can only shrink the gap.
The two-line derivation, with Jensen

Multiply and divide by \(q\) inside the integral, and use \(\log \E \ge \E \log\) from section 1.4:

\[ \log p_\theta(x) = \log \E_q\!\left[ \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)} \right] \;\ge\; \E_q\!\left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z)} \right]. \]

Quicker, but it only says the bound holds. The derivation above also says what the gap is.

The KL is an integral too. Have we really avoided integrating?

The integral we could not compute is the one over all latents, \(p_\theta(x) = \int p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)\, \d z\), and it hides inside the true posterior \(p_\theta(z \mid x)\). Look at where that posterior appears in the identity: only in the KL on the right, \(\KL\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big)\). That KL is exactly the term we set aside, using only the fact that it is never negative. We never compute it.

The ELBO that remains is still an expectation, but of a quantity we can evaluate at any \(z\), namely \(\log p_\theta(x, z) - \log q(z)\), and it is taken under \(q\), a distribution we chose so that we can sample from it. So we estimate it by drawing a few \(z\) from \(q\) and averaging, and when \(q\) and the prior are both Gaussian, its KL part has a closed form. The difference from before is not that integrals disappear, but that every one that is left can be estimated by sampling or written down exactly.

docs.title: How do we know the proxy is good?
docs.text:
We cannot compare \(q\) with the true posterior directly, because we do not have the true posterior. The identity helps here. Its left side does not depend on \(q\), so whenever a change to \(q\) raises the ELBO, the KL from \(q\) to the true posterior drops by exactly the same amount. In other words, maximising the ELBO over \(q\) minimises that KL, even though the KL itself cannot be computed.

This is the same move as in section 3. There the unknown was the data distribution, and the KL to it fell as an average over data rose. Here the unknown is the posterior, and the KL to it falls as the ELBO rises. In both cases an unknown constant is left over, so we can rank proxies but not read off how far the best one still is.

Does the gap ever actually close?

Only if the family of \(q\) contains the true posterior. In the example it does, because the true posterior is Gaussian; the explorer below lets you close the gap by hand. For a network decoder the true posterior is generally not Gaussian and a gap remains. In DDPM, the posteriors that matter are exactly Gaussian, which is one reason the method is so clean.

docs.title: 8. The ELBO as the training loss
docs.text:
Section 3 asked us to maximise \(\E_{\text{data}}[\log p_\theta(x)]\). Section 6 bounds \(\log p_\theta(x)\) from below for every data point, so it bounds the average too:

\[ \E_{x \sim \text{data}}\big[ \log p_\theta(x) \big] \;\ge\; \E_{x \sim \text{data}}\big[ \text{ELBO}(q_x, \theta) \big]. \]

The training objective

Maximise the average ELBO over the data, with respect to the model's parameters \(\theta\) and the proxies \(q\) together. In code: minimise \(-\text{ELBO}\).

Substitute \(p_\theta(x, z) = p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)\) and regroup:

\[ \text{ELBO} = \underbrace{\E_q\big[ \log p_\theta(x \mid z) \big]}_{\text{reconstruction}} \;-\; \underbrace{\KL\big( q(z) \,\|\, p(z) \big)}_{\text{penalty for leaving the prior}} . \]

Reconstruction is large when the latents proposed by \(q\) decode to something close to \(x\); on its own it would shrink \(q\) to a spike. The penalty is zero when \(q\) is the prior; on its own it would make \(q\) ignore \(x\). In the table, the prior has no penalty but poor reconstruction, the narrow guess reconstructs well but pays a heavy penalty, and the true posterior is the best compromise.

If the KL term pulls q towards the prior, what stops q from simply becoming the prior?

The reconstruction term does, and the optimiser needs no extra instruction to balance the two, because it only ever sees their sum. If \(q\) became the prior, the KL term would be zero, but \(q\) would then propose latents that have nothing to do with \(x\), the decoder would reconstruct \(x\) badly, and the reconstruction term would be very negative. Moving \(q\) away from the prior, towards the latents that actually explain \(x\), costs a little in the KL term and gains much more in reconstruction, so the sum goes up. The optimum is where one more step in either direction would lose more than it gains, and the table above shows that point: for this example it is exactly the true posterior.

Where squared error comes from. With a Gaussian decoder, \(\log p(x \mid z) = -\frac{(x - wz)^2}{2s^2} + \text{const}\). The reconstruction term is minus a squared error. Maximum likelihood with a Gaussian output is the same as least squares; the squared error was not chosen by hand.

What happens if we drop the KL term?

Then we have an ordinary autoencoder. Reconstruction becomes excellent, but each data point's latents end up in narrow, scattered spikes. A latent drawn from the prior lands between them, where the decoder was never trained, and decodes to garbage. The KL term keeps the region the encoder uses and the region the prior samples from the same.

Should the two terms be weighted against each other?

In the ELBO both have weight one, and that is what makes the sum a lower bound. In practice a weight \(\beta\) on the KL is common: \(\beta > 1\) holds \(q\) closer to the prior at the cost of reconstruction. That model is the \(\beta\)-VAE. It no longer bounds the likelihood, but it is often useful.

docs.title: 9. Where this goes next
docs.text:
Three facts carry forward.

  1. For any \(q\), \(\log p_\theta(x) = \text{ELBO} + \KL\big(q \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big)\).
  2. The ELBO splits into reconstruction and a KL to the prior; KLs between Gaussians are closed-form, and with equal variances they are squared distances between means.
  3. A Gaussian sample can be written as mean plus scale times standard noise, \(z = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon\).

Three changes turn this into DDPM:

VAE DDPM latents one, \(z\), usually smaller than \(x\) \(T\) of them, \(x_1, \ldots, x_T\), each the size of the data proxy \(q\) a learned network, the encoder fixed: add a little Gaussian noise at each step decoder one network, one step one network applied \(T\) times, each step removing a little noise

With a fixed proxy there is nothing to learn on that side, and with a chain of latents the single KL becomes a sum of KLs, one per step.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The numbers in the table come from this script. It computes the exact log-likelihood and posterior of the example, the ELBO in closed form and by sampling, and checks the identity.

"""Study step 1: a latent-variable model small enough to check the ELBO against the exact answer.

    latent     z ~ N(0, 1)
    decoder    x | z ~ N(w z, s^2)
so that        x ~ N(0, w^2 + s^2)                      (the marginal likelihood, exact)
and            z | x ~ N(w x / (w^2+s^2), s^2 / (w^2+s^2))   (the true posterior, exact)

For any Gaussian guess q(z) = N(m, v) the ELBO has a closed form, and
    log p(x) = ELBO(q) + KL(q || true posterior)        holds exactly.
"""
import numpy as np

w, s, x = 1.0, 0.8, 1.5


def log_normal(u, mean, var):
    return -0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * var) - (u - mean) ** 2 / (2 * var)


def exact():
    vx = w * w + s * s
    return log_normal(x, 0.0, vx), w * x / vx, s * s / vx          # log p(x), posterior mean, posterior variance


def elbo_closed_form(m, v):
    reconstruction = -0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * s * s) - ((x - w * m) ** 2 + w * w * v) / (2 * s * s)   # E_q[log p(x|z)]
    kl_to_prior = 0.5 * (v + m * m - 1.0 - np.log(v))                                                  # KL(q || N(0,1))
    return reconstruction - kl_to_prior, reconstruction, kl_to_prior


def elbo_monte_carlo(m, v, n=400_000, seed=0):
    z = m + np.sqrt(v) * np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(n)       # z ~ q
    return np.mean(log_normal(z, 0.0, 1.0) + log_normal(x, w * z, s * s) - log_normal(z, m, v))   # E_q[log p(x,z) - log q(z)]


def kl_gauss(m1, v1, m2, v2):
    return 0.5 * (np.log(v2 / v1) + (v1 + (m1 - m2) ** 2) / v2 - 1.0)


def prior_sampling_estimate(n, seed):
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(n)                        # z ~ prior
    return np.log(np.mean(np.exp(log_normal(x, w * z, s * s))))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logpx, pm, pv = exact()
    print(f"exact:  log p(x) = {logpx:.4f}    true posterior = N({pm:.4f}, {pv:.4f})")
    for name, (m, v) in {"q = prior N(0,1)": (0.0, 1.0), "q = N(1.5, 0.25)": (1.5, 0.25), "q = true posterior": (pm, pv)}.items():
        e, rec, klp = elbo_closed_form(m, v)
        gap = kl_gauss(m, v, pm, pv)
        print(f"{name:20s} ELBO = {e:.4f}  (reconstruction {rec:.4f}, KL to prior {klp:.4f})   "
              f"gap KL(q||posterior) = {gap:.4f}   ELBO + gap = {e + gap:.4f}   Monte Carlo ELBO = {elbo_monte_carlo(m, v):.4f}")
    print("estimating log p(x) by sampling z from the prior, 5 runs of 20 samples:   ",
          "  ".join(f"{prior_sampling_estimate(20, k):.3f}" for k in range(5)))
    print("same with 20000 samples:                                                  ",
          "  ".join(f"{prior_sampling_estimate(20000, k):.3f}" for k in range(5)))
